title: Red
passages:
The rig was scrub-white, which in the Interior meant it had been washed enough times to strip the node grime off its hull and leave nothing underneath but the metal and the company's nerve. It cranked into Anza's yard on low idle, tracks whispering over the cinders, and folded its claim-serve mast flat against the roof like a weapon surrendered at the gate. A line-trust officer rode scrub-white for a reason: the desk sent them when a node's trust score went red, and the desk did not send coffee.

Fenn climbed down. They wore the trust officer's grey coat with the brass buttons undone at the collar, and they carried a slate that did not flicker once as they crossed the yard. Both shifts were already at the board—Nour in her Shift 1 coveralls, Teodoro with his relay log tucked under one arm, V. Ospina leaning against the seal press with the chipped die still in their pocket, Rhea with her grease-stained hands tucked under her armpits because she had been at Ivo's bedside until ten minutes ago and had not bothered to warm up. Doan stood at the edge with their wrist looped in the overlap locker cord, even though the key was dead and the locker would not open.

Fenn stopped in front of the board and looked at the gathered faces.

"The morning desk at Kettering sends its terms," they said. "Anza's trust score is red. Resupply is frozen. Clearances are withdrawn. To reopen the line, the node does one of three things. It produces Calder Voss, the Bay 4 forger who resealed four rigs and dropped off Kettering's master board at 06:14. It hands over the living witness currently entered as crew on Anza's plate—Marlowe, countersigned by Ospina's seal authority. Or the resupply stays frozen through the winter, and Anza eats what it has until it doesn't."

Teodoro said, "That's not terms. That's a menu with no prices."

Nour's tally card lay face-out on the board ledge, eleven seals short across four down-line runs. She did not look at it. She looked at Fenn. "The desk knows Voss is gone. They know we don't have him."

"They know we have Marlowe," Fenn said. "A living witness with a name and a bunk. The desk will take a body it can read over a name it can't."

Ospina pushed off the seal press. "Marlowe's not cargo. He's crew. You can't serve a serve order on a listed bunk."

"I can," Fenn said, and tapped the slate. "A hands claim is still active. The desk doesn't care whose name is on the plate if the hands are still on the manifest. I serve first light. Either Voss walks through that gate, or Marlowe walks to my rig."

Rhea said, "My brother's on four respirator cartridges. If you freeze the compressor to make your point, I'll turn this board into kindling."

"Then hope the forger turns up first," Fenn said. "Because I don't drop a thread. Not for a node, not for a brother, and not for a man who counted someone down to a lid and vanished."

They turned the slate face-down on the board. The mast on their rig clicked once, unfolding a half-notch, hungry and ready.

Fenn didn't wait for an answer. They turned their slate toward the claim-serve mast on their rig and fed Anza's node code into the reader. The mast clicked again, unfolding another notch, and the yard lights dimmed.

"That's the ore stub's trace heating," Doan said, their wrist still looped in the locker cord. "You cut that, the fines freeze in the chute. Next shift can't move a ton."

"Next shift can eat what we have or starve," Fenn said. "The desk doesn't run a node on good intentions."

They tapped the slate once more. Somewhere inside the relay shop, a breaker tripped. The fluorescent strip over the board flickered once, then settled to a sickly green. The relay shop was now on a brown-out rota—a power-cut schedule that cycled each circuit off for as long as it stayed on. Which meant Ivo's respirator compressor, the box that pushed filtered air through the patch on his diaphragm, was on a two-hour cycle.

Rhea didn't wait for the explanation. She had already left Ivo's bedside, and she pulled a spent cartridge from her coverall pocket—a scrubber canister that cleaned the air before it reached the mask—and snapped it against her palm like she was cracking an egg.

"Four cartridges," she said, loud enough for the board, for Teodoro, for Nour, for Ospina with the chipped die in their pocket, for Doan with their dead key. "Six hours of run time each. That's twenty-four hours. Your brown-out rota gives the compressor two hours on, two hours off. Twenty-four hours of run time stretched across a fifty-percent duty cycle is forty-eight hours of clock time. You haven't cut Ivo's air to zero. You've given us two days."

She snapped the cartridge again.

"But the diaphragm is patched with glove rubber. Every time that motor spools up from a dead stop, it pulls a vacuum before the seal holds. That vacuum burns a quarter cartridge per start. Twelve starts in forty-eight hours. Three cartridges gone just to re-pressurize. One cartridge left. Six hours of actual breathing. So your clean board buys us until nightfall, not until morning. Do the math, officer. Then tell me which one of them—Voss or Marlowe—can run a compressor on cold cinders."

Fenn's slate chimed. Another shed notice, this one for the med rig Rhea had towed in dead and untraceable. The rig had no transponder, no power draw, nothing to cut—but the alert still blinked red on Fenn's screen.

"Your rig's dead," Rhea said. "You're shedding load off a ghost."

"I'm shedding load until the desk sees a clean board," Fenn said. "And right now your board is dirty."

The relay shop's alarm chirped—a low, dying tone. The compressor had just cycled off. Somewhere behind the board wall, Ivo was holding his breath.

Rhea was already moving. She got a hand under Ivo's jaw, tipped the mask to seat, and squeezed the manual bulb at the base of the collar—a rubber squeeze-bag, the backup you pumped by hand when the motor quit. Three hard pushes. Ivo's chest lifted.

"You've got real timing," Ivo said around the mask, voice thin and flat, the patch doing half a lung's work. "Walking a company man in on the off-cycle."

"Breathe," Rhea said.

She brought Fenn in without asking. The relay shop was one long room behind the board wall, cable trays overhead, the compressor caged under Ivo's cot—a squat grey box with a pull-cord, dead and ticking as it cooled. The green strip light made everyone look drowned. She pulled a maintenance slate from her coverall, the kind that jacks into a rig's spine and reads back everything the machine saw, and dropped it on the blanket by Ivo's hip.

"That's the med rig I towed in dead. Watch the trace." A flat green line ran across the screen. "That's the databus—the wire bundle every sensor on the rig talks over. Somebody cut it here." She tapped a clean gap in the line. "After that the rig went dumb. Last thing it believed was thirty-six point four degrees. Cabin temp, steady. That's the repeater—the box that keeps shouting the last good number when the real sensors go quiet. It held thirty-six point four the whole way in from Kettering."

"So it held a number," Fenn said.

"There was a man sealed in that box. The rig swore he was warm start to finish. It lied with a straight face, and your desk reads plates the same way—takes the number, never looks in the box." She thumbed the bulb again. Ivo coughed, wet. "The whole Kettering record's got a cut wire running through it. Marlowe's down as cargo because a dead truck said so."

"A machine's memory is not a person's word," Fenn said.

Rhea's jaw worked. "Good thing I don't need it to be a person. I need it to be a reason."

"Then you've got a reason and I've got a rota." Fenn crouched, looked at the compressor in its cage, then at the bulb in her fist. "A cut databus is a fault. Faults happen on this line every hour of every shift. It tells me a rig broke. It doesn't tell me who Marlowe is, or what he's owed, or why the desk should thaw a red node for a man a machine already wrote off. You brought me a ghost, Rhea. I don't clear boards with ghosts."

"Then what do you clear them with."

"A signature." Fenn stood and laid two fingers on the compressor's pull-cord—not pulling, just resting them there, a man at a door. "The rota takes this box two hours off, two hours on. It doesn't have to. I restore the compressor's priority—full time, corded straight to the shop main, off the cycle—the same hour you sign the witness over. Marlowe walks to my rig at first light. Your brother breathes till spring."

Ivo's hand came up off the blanket and closed on Rhea's sleeve. She didn't look down at him.

"You'd trade a man you never met for a box that keeps me going," Ivo said, mild as anything, "and call that a clean board."

"I'd call it arithmetic." Fenn's fingers stayed on the cord. "One cartridge left, you said. Six hours. But every time this box coughs awake it eats a quarter of that just to seal, and you've watched it cough twice since I walked in. Keep it on my rota and you'll spend your six hours on restarts, pumping that bulb in the gaps, watching him go grey. Sign, and it runs clean—no starts, no gaps. Your call, mechanic. But make it before the next off-cycle. I'm not standing here working that bulb for you."

Fenn found the relay bunk off the board wall, a narrow room with three cots and a locker that smelled of copper and old sweat. Marlowe lay on the middle cot, one arm over his eyes, his shoulder splinted with cardboard and tape. Fenn set a handheld on the floor and unfolded its wire antenna, which clicked into the node’s carrier signal.

“You’re Marlowe,” Fenn said. “Bay 4, Shift 2. Sealed inside as ballast. Kettering’s plate reads cargo. Anza’s plate reads crew. Which one are you?”

Marlowe uncovered one eye. “Depends who’s asking. You a line-trust officer or a bill collector?”

“Line-trust. Fenn.” Fenn tapped the slate. “I need your statement. The med rig’s databus trace says you were warm in the box. I know you weren’t. Tell me what happened between the lid going down and the lid staying down.”

Marlowe laughed, then winced, pressing a hand to his splinted shoulder. “Between the lid and the lid. Cute. Trust officers always sound like they’re reading off a warning label.”

“Tell me anyway.”

“The first pair of hands was Calder Voss. Bay 4 forger. He had the stamp, the ink, the chipped die. He stamped the manifest while I stood there holding my own lungs. But the hands that closed the box—” Marlowe thumbed his own knuckle. “Those weren’t his. Taped knuckles. Grey tape, the kind you wrap around rig cables when the insulation cracks. I didn’t see a face. I felt the tape when they shoved my head down into the foam. They held the lid while they counted aloud. Three, two, one. Then Voss stamped it closed.”

“Smell?” Fenn said.

“Ozone and hydraulic fluid, cold enough to freeze the grease, and something sweet, like rotten fruit in a warm cab.”

Fenn keyed the handheld. “Taped knuckle. Count to lid. Smell profile. Got it.”

The device chimed—a low, three-note ripple. A red tag blinked on the screen: HANDS CLAIM ACTIVE. MARLOWE, UNRESOLVED.

“Still active,” Fenn said. “The desk’s manifest still carries your name under ballast. That claim hasn’t been cleared.”

“Because nobody wants to clear it,” Marlowe said. “They want me gone, not found. There’s a difference.”

“The desk wants you served at first light. My rig, the gate, no arguments.”

Marlowe sat up, the cot springs groaning. “And if I give you the second pair of hands? The taped knuckle? That’s a name you can serve instead of me.”

“It’s a description,” Fenn said. “Descriptions don’t walk through gates.”

“They do if the desk runs facial trace.” Marlowe held up his splinted arm. “I can’t lift a crate with this shoulder, but I can remember a face. The second one was shorter than Voss. Wore a coat with Kettering’s brass on the collar. Smelled like that rotten fruit. You want a forger? Voss is your forger. You want the hands that counted me down? That’s someone else. Someone still on the line.”

Fenn looked at the handheld. The claim tag pulsed. They could key a single sequence, log Marlowe’s words as sworn testimony, and the claim would lock into a serve order with Marlowe’s name attached. Instead, Fenn closed the slate without saving.

“I’m not logging it,” Fenn said.

“Why not?”

“Because if I log it, the desk owns the record. And if the desk owns the record, they don’t need me to serve you. They can send a crew with a warrant and take you before dawn, no rota, no bargaining. You give me the name of the second pair, I put it on my slate, not Kettering’s. That’s the only protection I can offer.”

Marlowe studied them. “You’re a strange kind of company man.”

“I’m the kind that doesn’t close threads until I have to,” Fenn said. “Get some rest. First light comes fast.”

Fenn turned for the door. The handheld chimed again in their pocket—a restricted burst, no text. A reclamation unit had just been assigned to Anza’s node code: unresolved ballast, physical recovery authorized, estimated arrival before morning. The desk wasn’t waiting for Fenn’s signature. It was already sending someone to take Marlowe by force.

Fenn stopped with their hand on the latch.
